props.text: What we learned moving 40 services to one queue
Consolidating six message brokers onto a single partitioned log cut our on-call pages by 60 percent. It also broke three things we didn't know were load-bearing.
Forty producers, one partitioned log. Illustration by the author.

Two years ago, a single customer import could wake up four teams. Each of our 40 services had picked its own broker at the time it was written: RabbitMQ here, SQS there, a Redis list that started as a prototype and never stopped being one. Every outage looked different, and none of them were anyone's fault.

So we made a bet: every asynchronous message in the company would flow through one partitioned log, owned by the platform team, with one set of dashboards and one runbook. This post is about what that migration taught us, including the parts we would do differently.
One queue, many shapes of work

The first surprise was how little our messages had in common. Billing events were tiny and strictly ordered per account. Search reindex jobs were enormous and didn't care about order at all. Notification fan-out was bursty: nothing for an hour, then two million messages in ninety seconds. A single queue had to treat all of them fairly without letting one starve the rest.
Consolidation doesn't remove complexity. It moves it to one place, where you can finally see it.

The fix was to stop partitioning by producer. Ordering only ever mattered within a tenant, so we hashed on the tenant id and gave every message a time budget. A consumer that blows its budget hands the message to a dead-letter partition instead of holding up everything behind it.

Twelve lines of routing replaced roughly four thousand lines of per-broker glue. The interesting work moved into the budget: picking it per message type, and alerting when a type spends more than half of it on a normal day.
What we'd tell ourselves two years ago
The migration took eleven months, not the four we planned. If we started over tomorrow, three rules would come first:

Today the queue moves about 1.8 billion messages a day. Most weeks nobody thinks about it, which was the whole point. Next month we'll write about the part we skipped here: replaying a week of traffic to prove the new system matched the old one.

value: Partition by what must stay in order, not by who sent the message. For us that was always the tenant.
Give every message type a time budget on day one, and alert on how much of it a normal day spends.
Migrate the noisiest producer first. Its edge cases become everyone's test suite for free.
